dataNotes.radius: Mean radius in kilometres, from JPL Planetary Satellite Physical Parameters. Small moons are not perfect spheres.
dataNotes.orbit: Rounded reference semimajor axes measure from the parent planet's centre, not its cloud tops. Periods are sidereal orbital periods in Earth days, not the interval between phases. These support an illustrative orbital model; they are not a live ephemeris.
dataNotes.editorial: The Europa ocean is strongly supported by evidence but has not been visited. Enceladus's global ocean is inferred from gravity, wobble and plume measurements. No life has been detected on either moon. Avoid calling Mimas frozen solid: its interior remains an active research topic. Render any asteroid-belt dots as an enlarged illustrative sample, not literal crowding.

moon.title: The Moon
moon.lead: Our nearest world, holding the marks of ancient impacts.
moon.description: Bright highlands surround dark plains of ancient lava. The Moon turns once during each journey around Earth, keeping the same side towards us.

stories.title: The far side has sunshine too.
stories.text: We usually see the same side of the Moon because its turn and its orbit take the same time. The hidden side still has day and night. It is a far side, not a permanently dark side.

stories.title: Footsteps that stay.
stories.text: There is no wind or rain to wash away the astronauts’ tracks. A spacecraft orbiting the Moon has photographed the trails they left decades ago.

io.title: Io
io.lead: A small world constantly rebuilding itself with volcanoes.
io.description: Yellow, orange and dark volcanic deposits cover Io. Jupiter and neighbouring moons keep flexing its interior, helping power the most active volcanoes in the solar system.

stories.title: Hundreds of volcanoes.
stories.text: Io has hundreds of volcanoes. Fresh lava keeps covering old ground and filling impact craters. A map of this moon can change while we are watching.

stories.title: Tides in solid ground.
stories.text: Jupiter’s pull can make Io’s rocky surface rise and fall by about 100 metres. Imagine the ground beneath you lifting as high as a tall building. All that flexing heats the moon inside.

stories.title: Fountains made of lava.
stories.text: Some of Io’s volcanoes throw fountains of lava kilometres into the sky. Imagine a fountain whose spray is glowing rock. Io may be small, but its eruptions are enormous.

europa.title: Europa
europa.lead: A cracked shell of ice, with an ocean hidden underneath.
europa.description: Long brown lines cross Europa’s bright ice. Measurements strongly suggest a deep, salty ocean beneath the frozen surface, making this moon an important place to explore.

stories.title: More ocean than Earth.
stories.text: Europa is smaller than our Moon, yet its hidden ocean may hold more than twice as much water as all Earth’s oceans together. Scientists are investigating whether conditions there could support life. No life has been found.

stories.title: An enormous ice puzzle.
stories.text: Some dark bands have edges that fit together like jigsaw pieces. They suggest that Europa’s icy shell has cracked and moved apart, with new material filling the gaps.

stories.title: A moon that gets squeezed warm.
stories.text: Jupiter’s gravity stretches and relaxes Europa as it goes around. This repeated flexing creates heat inside. Even far from the Sun, a frozen surface can hide liquid water below.

ganymede.title: Ganymede
ganymede.lead: The largest moon, with bright ice and its own magnetic field.
ganymede.description: Dark old terrain meets lighter bands of grooved ice. Ganymede is larger than Mercury, and its magnetic field helps create glowing auroras near the poles.

stories.title: A moon bigger than a planet.
stories.text: Ganymede is wider than Mercury. It is still a moon because it travels around Jupiter. A world’s size alone does not tell you whether it is a planet or a moon.

stories.title: Northern lights on a moon.
stories.text: Ganymede is the only moon known to make its own magnetic field. Glowing bands of gas form near its poles, rather like Earth’s northern and southern lights.

stories.title: One, two, four. A rhythm in space.
stories.text: While Ganymede makes one trip around Jupiter, Europa makes two and Io makes four. Their repeated gravitational tugs help keep this remarkable rhythm. Try counting the trips in their orrery.

callisto.title: Callisto
callisto.lead: An ancient world that remembers countless collisions.
callisto.description: Bright impact marks cover Callisto’s dark mixture of ice and rock. Much of this surface has survived for billions of years, preserving clues to the early solar system.

stories.title: A history written in craters.
stories.text: Callisto’s surface is billions of years old and crowded with impact craters. Each scar marks a collision. With little resurfacing to erase them, the moon keeps a very long memory.

stories.title: The mark of one enormous splash.
stories.text: A huge impact left the Valhalla basin surrounded by circles in the crust. They look a little like ripples spreading from a stone dropped into a pond, frozen into the landscape.

titan.title: Titan
titan.lead: Orange skies above rivers, lakes and seas of methane.
titan.description: Titan’s thick atmosphere hides an icy landscape. Its clouds can rain liquid methane, which flows across the ground and gathers in lakes and seas.

stories.title: Rain made of something else.
stories.text: Titan has clouds, rain and rivers, but its rain is methane. Here on warm Earth, methane is a gas. Titan is so cold that it can flow like water.

stories.title: A robot bounced here.
stories.text: The Huygens probe landed on Titan in 2005. Scientists worked out that it bounced, slid and wobbled before coming to rest. Its pictures gave us a view from beneath the orange haze.

stories.title: Here, ice is the rock.
stories.text: Titan is about −179°C at the surface. Water ice stays so hard that it plays the part of rock in the landscape. The rivers flowing over that frozen ground are made of liquid methane and ethane.

enceladus.title: Enceladus
enceladus.lead: A bright little moon spraying ocean material into space.
enceladus.description: Enceladus has a frozen white surface and a global ocean underneath. Near its south pole, long cracks release jets of water vapour and tiny grains of ice.

stories.title: An ocean we can sample from space.
stories.text: Jets burst from cracks called tiger stripes. Cassini flew through the spray and sampled material from the hidden ocean. It found ingredients useful for life, but no evidence of living things.

stories.title: A moon that feeds a ring.
stories.text: Some ice grains escape Enceladus and spread around Saturn. They help make the faint E ring. This tiny moon keeps adding fresh material to an enormous ring.

stories.title: Hot springs beneath a frozen world.
stories.text: Tiny grains found by Cassini suggest that hot water meets rock deep beneath the ice. Scientists think Enceladus may have hot springs on its ocean floor, far below the freezing surface.

mimas.title: Mimas
mimas.lead: A small icy moon with one astonishingly large crater.
mimas.description: Mimas is covered in impact scars. The largest, Herschel, takes up a striking part of its face, with steep walls and a mountain rising from the middle.

stories.title: An impact it almost did not survive.
stories.text: Herschel crater is about 130 kilometres wide, roughly a third of Mimas’s diameter. The collision that made it may have come close to breaking the little moon apart.

stories.title: Around Saturn before tomorrow.
stories.text: Mimas completes an orbit in about 23 hours. It could make one whole trip around Saturn between one morning on Earth and the next, always keeping the same face towards the planet.

rhea.title: Rhea
rhea.lead: A frozen world crossed by bright cliffs of ice.
rhea.description: Saturn’s second-largest moon has a surface rich in water ice. Ancient craters and bright fracture walls record a history of impacts and cracking.

stories.title: Ice that behaves like rock.
stories.text: Rhea is so cold that its water ice acts like hard rock. Bright lines once looked like wisps in distant pictures. Close-up images revealed steep, shining walls of ice.

stories.title: Oxygen, but no air to breathe.
stories.text: Cassini found a very thin cloud of oxygen and carbon dioxide around Rhea. The oxygen is trillions of times less dense than on Earth. Finding oxygen does not always mean finding breathable air.

iapetus.title: Iapetus
iapetus.lead: A two-tone moon with mountains along its middle.
iapetus.description: One side of Iapetus is much darker than the other. Along part of its equator, a strange ridge makes the moon resemble a walnut with a raised seam.

stories.title: A mountain seam around a moon.
stories.text: A line of mountains follows part of Iapetus’s equator. Some rise about ten kilometres. Scientists are still debating how this unusual ridge formed.

stories.title: Dark ground gets darker.
stories.text: Dark material absorbs more sunshine than bright ice. On Iapetus, that extra warmth helps ice escape from darker places and settle in colder ones, making the contrast even stronger.

dione.title: Dione
dione.lead: A moon of ice cliffs travelling with two tiny companions.
dione.description: Bright fractures cut across Dione’s cratered surface. Two smaller moons share its path around Saturn, one travelling ahead and the other behind.

stories.title: Lines that became cliffs.
stories.text: From far away, Dione’s bright markings looked like delicate streaks. Cassini came closer and found canyon walls hundreds of metres high, where clean ice shines through darker dust.

stories.title: Three moons on one track.
stories.text: Dione shares its orbit with little Helene and Polydeuces. One travels about a sixth of a circle ahead; the other trails behind. Gravity keeps them near these special places.

tethys.title: Tethys
tethys.lead: An icy moon split by a valley more than half a world long.
tethys.description: Tethys has two enormous landmarks: a broad, shallow impact crater and the long valley called Ithaca Chasma. Both record dramatic events in this moon’s past.

stories.title: A valley 2,000 kilometres long.
stories.text: Ithaca Chasma stretches roughly 2,000 kilometres across Tethys. It is so long that it reaches more than halfway around this little moon. Scientists are still working out what split the ice.

stories.title: A crater almost half a moon wide.
stories.text: Odysseus crater is about 400 kilometres across, nearly two-fifths of Tethys’s width. Its walls have slumped over time, leaving a shallow bowl where a huge collision once struck.

belt.title: The asteroid belt
belt.lead: Ancient pieces of the solar system, separated by enormous distances.
belt.description: Between Mars and Jupiter, rocky objects travel on their own paths around the Sun. Most are small and irregular. The region also contains the dwarf planet Ceres and the large asteroid Vesta.
belt.renderingNote: These bounds are a convenient illustration of the main belt, not sharp edges. Dots should be sparse, enlarged and explicitly labelled as an illustrative sample. Individual asteroid locations are not live positions.

stories.title: Mostly empty space.
stories.text: The belt is enormously spread out. Large asteroids can be millions of kilometres apart. A spacecraft usually crosses without weaving between rocks: finding an asteroid to visit takes careful aiming.

stories.title: There is a dwarf planet here.
stories.text: Ceres is the biggest object in the belt. It is a whole round world, classed as a dwarf planet. NASA’s Dawn spacecraft reached it in 2015 after first exploring Vesta.

stories.title: Pieces of Vesta reached Earth.
stories.text: Some meteorites found on Earth appear to have come from Vesta. Collisions knocked pieces into space long ago. Scientists can study those rocks here as well as pictures taken beside the asteroid.
